title: Vortex rings as hydrodynamic dispersants for mitigating underwater oil spills
authors: Siddhant Jain, Saini Jatin Rao, Saptarshi Basu
abstract: The usage of chemical dispersant to promote the breakup of oil droplets remains one of the crucial response strategy towards controlling the rapidly rising droplets during an underwater oil spillage disaster like the Deepwater horizon. However, the detrimental effects of dispersant on the marine life are now well recognized. Here, we demonstrate that vortex ring presents an environmental friendly alternative to the debatable usage of chemical dispersant that primarily aids droplet break-up. We propose two mitigating strategies through the application of vortex rings: (i) atomization of large oil droplets into smaller droplets, which enhances natural dispersion and biodegradation (ii) targeted relocation of spilled oil droplets from ecologically sensitive regions to safer remote locations during minor spill events. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that vortex rings can efficiently atomize underwater oil droplets while simultaneously transporting them over long distances. The efficiency strongly depends on the droplet size distribution and the strength of the vortex ring. Using time scale analysis and force balances arguments, we propose droplet response and atomization criteria by a traversing vortex ring. Beyond atomization and droplet transport which are center to many engineering processes, the work finds high relevance in the area of bubble turbulence, agricultural industry, multiphase reactors, combustion process, atmospheric fluid dynamics and oil extraction from rocks, to name a few.

infographic.key_insight: Traversing vortex rings can replace chemical dispersants by both breaking large underwater oil droplets into smaller ones and relocating droplets away from sensitive areas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a potentially eco-friendlier flow-control tool for spill response and also informs multiphase technologies that rely on droplet breakup and transport.
method: Generate vortex rings and send them through submerged oil droplets.
Use ring strength and droplet-size distribution to tune breakup vs. transport behavior.
Apply time-scale analysis and force-balance criteria to predict droplet response and atomization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a proof-of-concept study showing vortex rings can efficiently atomize underwater oil droplets and transport them over long distances.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends strongly on droplet size distribution and vortex-ring strength, so field deployment would need careful tuning and validation.
infographic.paper_title: Vortex rings as hydrodynamic dispersants for mitigating underwater oil spills

title: Airfoil2Vec: Spectral Geometry-Conditioned Neural Surrogate Models for Airfoil Aerodynamics and a Downforce-Generating CFD Dataset
authors: Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde, Flavio Savarino, Andrei Cristian Popescu, Pietro Innocenzi, Pantelis Papageorgiou, Xerxes Xian Chong
abstract: We introduce a dataset of approximately 10,000 Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations of steady, incompressible, two-dimensional subsonic flow around downforce-generating NACA 4-digit airfoils, targeting aerodynamic regimes relevant to automotive and motorsport applications (openly available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/ratiolabs/downforce-airfoils). Using this resource, we study geometry-conditioned neural surrogates for fast flow prediction, comparing neural fields with neural ODEs, MLPs with graph-based models, and several spectral geometry-conditioning methods. We further propose Airfoil2Vec, an airfoil-specific spectral geometry encoder that combines the joint contour spectrum with separate spectral representations of camber and thickness, for predicting continuous pressure and velocity fields. We evaluate generalization through angle-of-attack interpolation, interpolation and extrapolation to unseen NACA 4-digit geometries, and generalization to unseen non-NACA airfoils. The resulting surrogate accurately captures aerodynamic quantities and qualitative flow features while providing orders-of-magnitude speedups over conventional computational fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Airfoil2Vec uses spectral geometry encoding to make neural surrogates predict airfoil flow fields much faster while staying accurate across new shapes and angles of attack.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables rapid aerodynamic screening for motorsport and automotive downforce design, reducing reliance on expensive CFD runs.
method: ~10,000 steady 2D RANS simulations of NACA 4-digit downforce airfoils form the dataset.
Airfoil2Vec combines the joint contour spectrum with separate spectral encodings of camber and thickness.
Models are tested against neural fields, neural ODEs, MLPs, graph models, and other spectral conditioning methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong generalization on angle-of-attack interpolation, unseen NACA geometries, and unseen non-NACA airfoils, with orders-of-magnitude speedups over CFD.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the learned geometry encoding transfers to airfoils outside the training distribution or to conditions beyond steady, incompressible 2D RANS.
infographic.paper_title: Airfoil2Vec: Spectral Geometry-Conditioned Neural Surrogate Models for Airfoil Aerodynamics and a Downforce-Generating CFD Dataset

title: Stable and Interpretable Multi-Mode Rheological Universal Differential Equations (mmRUDEs) for Data-Driven Constitutive Modeling
authors: Mohua Das, Nicholas King, Navid Azizan, Gareth H. McKinley
abstract: The Rheological Universal Differential Equation (RUDE) framework embeds neural networks within a frame-indifferent tensorial constitutive backbone and so enables data-driven discovery of complex material rheological behavior. However, the flexibility that makes the RUDE framework attractive also makes it difficult to deploy: the learned neural network correction can make the constitutive equation numerically stiff during training, distribute corrections across non-unique combinations of tensor-basis terms, and extrapolate poorly with increasing nonlinearity, especially for industrially relevant materials with broad relaxation spectra. We develop a stability- and reliability-focused multi-mode RUDE framework that addresses three key challenges: thermodynamic admissibility, out-of-distribution prediction, and interpretability. Logarithmic compression of the input invariants and a split-network architecture improve numerical conditioning during training, while a differentiable projection layer enforces the Clausius--Duhem inequality at every time step. We illustrate the framework with both synthetic (a multi-mode Giesekus model) and experimental data on an entangled silicone polymer melt. Both models were trained on LAOS; they remain stable and accurate under unseen flow conditions, including steady shear, transient stress growth, and extensional flows, for which the unconstrained models may diverge numerically. To aid in interpretation of the contributions of each learned correction to the rheological behavior, we introduce the rheome, a compact way of representing the dominant weighted tensor-basis contributions to the overall rheological behavior. These improvements to the RUDE framework lead to stable and interpretable trained models, paving the way for implementation in computational fluid dynamics simulations and for guiding the rational design of soft material processing operations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper stabilizes neural constitutive modeling by combining a multi-mode RUDE backbone with conditioning, thermodynamic constraints, and an interpretable summary of learned tensor contributions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables reliable, data-driven rheology models that can be used in CFD and process design for complex soft materials under unseen flow conditions.
method: Log-compress input invariants and use a split-network architecture to improve training conditioning.
Add a differentiable projection layer to enforce the Clausius–Duhem inequality at every time step.
Introduce the “rheome” to compactly visualize dominant weighted tensor-basis contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was trained on LAOS data and validated on both synthetic multi-mode Giesekus data and experimental entangled silicone polymer melt data, where it stayed stable and accurate on unseen shear, stress-growth, and extensional flows.
infographic.watch_item: The added constraints and projection layer improve robustness, but implementation may be more complex and performance still depends on the quality and breadth of the training data.
infographic.paper_title: Stable and Interpretable Multi-Mode Rheological Universal Differential Equations (mmRUDEs) for Data-Driven Constitutive Modeling

title: Reconstruction of Molten Pool Flow Fields from High-Speed Video Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Yue Cao, Qin Su, Dung Hoang Tien, Van Anh Nguyen
abstract: Molten pool flow significantly influences bead geometry, defect formation, and solidification microstructure in wire-arc directed energy deposition (DED). However, direct flow sensing remains an open challenge due to extreme temperatures, intense arc illumination, and complex flow patterns. Traditional research has relied either on computationally intensive fluid dynamics simulations, which require assumed boundary conditions and lack empirical anchoring, or on vision-based tracer particle tracking, which yields sparse, noisy, and physically unconstrained velocity estimates. This work bridges these two paradigms by reconstructing physics-constrained 2D surface flow fields from high-speed imaging of a GTAW-based wire-arc DED process under distinct flow regimes: quasi-steady convection and periodic droplet impact. The pipeline begins with homography correction to calibrate the oblique camera view, followed by dense optical flow extraction to provide raw velocity observations. For quasi-steady pools, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) reconstructs the surface velocity field by jointly enforcing data fidelity, incompressible Navier-Stokes momentum equations, no-penetration boundary conditions, and an arc-forcing prior through composite loss minimization. For pools subject to periodic droplet impact, a phase-conditioned time-dependent PINN is further developed to resolve the cyclic flow evolution throughout the impact period. This work provides a unified framework that bridges high-speed visual sensing and fluid mechanics, enabling physics-grounded flow diagnostics for wire-arc DED processes.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reconstructs molten-pool surface flow fields from high-speed video by combining optical-flow measurements with physics-informed neural networks that enforce fluid dynamics constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable, physically grounded monitoring of wire-arc DED melt-pool behavior, which can improve bead geometry control, defect prevention, and microstructure consistency.
method: Homography-corrected high-speed images are converted into dense optical-flow velocity observations.
A PINN reconstructs quasi-steady surface flow by minimizing data error plus incompressible Navier–Stokes and no-penetration boundary losses.
For droplet-impact cases, a phase-conditioned time-dependent PINN captures cyclic flow evolution over the impact period.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on high-speed video from a GTAW-based wire-arc DED process under two regimes: quasi-steady convection and periodic droplet impact.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy may depend on camera calibration, optical-flow quality, and how well the assumed 2D surface-flow and boundary-condition priors match the real melt pool.
infographic.paper_title: Reconstruction of Molten Pool Flow Fields from High-Speed Video Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: Physics-Informed Method of Group Data Handling: Adaptive Construction of Functional Representations with an Application to the Navier-Stokes Equations
authors: Mykhailo Minin
abstract: Physics-informed computational methods usually optimize parameters within a functional representation whose structure is fixed in advance. This work proposes a Physics-Informed Method of Group Data Handling (PI-GMDH), in which representations of coupled physical fields are progressively constructed during solution. Candidate functional directions are evaluated through the first variation of the complete physical and observational objective, introduced in packages, and followed by block-coordinate damped Gauss-Newton coefficient optimization. The framework is demonstrated with tensor-product Chebyshev functions on the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations using a two-dimensional time-dependent Taylor-Green benchmark. Under the tested configuration, adaptive PI-GMDH reached validation and held-out test losses of 5.299e-19 and 5.296e-19 with 204, 201, and 175 active functions for u, v, and p. Complete degree-by-degree and all-terms PI-GMDH variants, together with selected PINN and KAN reference configurations, are used to examine the effect of structural construction policy. The results show that, for this controlled synthetic benchmark, selective progressive construction can provide a favorable combination of accuracy, representation size, and wall-clock time. The comparison is illustrative rather than a claim of universal superiority over alternative physics-informed approaches.

infographic.key_insight: PI-GMDH adaptively builds the functional form of physics-informed representations during training, rather than fixing the architecture upfront, and applies it to incompressible Navier-Stokes flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can reduce model size and training cost while preserving high accuracy for fluid-flow surrogates and inverse/forward physics-informed simulation workflows.
method: Generate candidate functional directions progressively using the first variation of the combined physics and data objective.
Optimize coefficients with block-coordinate damped Gauss-Newton updates.
Use tensor-product Chebyshev basis functions for the 2D time-dependent Taylor-Green Navier-Stokes benchmark.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the Taylor-Green benchmark, adaptive PI-GMDH achieved validation and held-out test losses of 5.299e-19 and 5.296e-19, with 204/201/175 active functions for u/v/p.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a controlled synthetic benchmark, so the apparent gains may not directly transfer to more complex or noisy real-world CFD problems.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Method of Group Data Handling: Adaptive Construction of Functional Representations with an Application to the Navier-Stokes Equations

title: Is Vorticity Amplification Essential for Anomalous Dissipation and Intermittency in Turbulence?
authors: Alessandro Chiarini
abstract: The distinct dynamical roles of vorticity amplification (VA) and vortex tilting (VT) in three-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence are investigated using direct numerical simulations of a modified Navier--Stokes system. By selectively suppressing VA while retaining VT, we demonstrate that gradient amplification by VA is strictly required to sustain the classical forward energy cascade. Progressively suppressing VA weakens small-scale velocity gradients, heavily depletes extreme fluctuations, and entirely eliminates the classical energy dissipative anomaly, causing the normalized energy dissipation to decay as $Re_λ^{-1}$. In the limit of complete VA suppression, enstrophy emerges as the relevant inviscid invariant. Scale-by-scale budget analyses confirm that the dynamics transition to a purely forward enstrophy cascade, characterized by an anomalous enstrophy dissipation and a robust $E(k) \sim k^{-3}$ intermediate energy spectrum. We verify that these asymptotic scaling limits---including a $Re_λ^{-1/2}$ finite-Reynolds-number correction for the enstrophy anomalous dissipation---are universal properties of the VA-suppressed dynamics, independent of whether the large-scale forcing is helical or non-helical. Remarkably, despite the smoothing of the velocity field and the elimination of the energy dissipative anomaly, anomalous structural scaling and a broad multifractal spectrum persist. These results reveal a fundamental mechanistic separation: while VA is responsible for amplifying intense localized fluctuations, geometric reorganization by VT alone is mechanically sufficient to sustain multifractal intermittency.

infographic.key_insight: Suppressing vorticity amplification breaks the classical energy cascade and dissipative anomaly, but vortex tilting alone can still sustain multifractal intermittency through a transition to an enstrophy-cascade regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result clarifies which nonlinear mechanisms control extreme gradients and dissipation in turbulence models, informing subgrid closures and flow-control strategies that target anomalous small-scale activity.
method: Direct numerical simulations of a modified 3D Navier--Stokes system
Selective suppression of vorticity amplification while retaining vortex tilting
Comparison across forcing types and Reynolds numbers using scale-by-scale budget analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that normalized energy dissipation decays as Re_λ^-1 under VA suppression, with universal Re_λ^-1/2 finite-Re corrections for anomalous enstrophy dissipation and a robust E(k) ~ k^-3 spectrum.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are drawn from an idealized modified Navier--Stokes setting, so translating them to real flows or turbulence models requires caution about implementation details and forcing dependence.
infographic.paper_title: Is Vorticity Amplification Essential for Anomalous Dissipation and Intermittency in Turbulence?

title: Microscopic origin of the chiral pressure in a two-dimensional fluid
authors: Francisco Vega Reyes
abstract: We show that a two-dimensional chiral fluid supports an antisymmetric contribution to the pressure, and determine its microscopic expression. Its origin lies outside the standard kinetic and collisional channels of the normal pressure tensor, stemming instead from the average of a parity-breaking pseudo-scalar. This chiral pressure is set by the rotational (vortex) viscosity of micropolar hydrodynamics, whose kinetic value for rough disks we compute here, to Gaussian order. Crucially, both the chiral pressure and the rotational viscosity survive at zeroth order in the gradients, meaning they persist even in the fully homogeneous fluid -- which we show is not only well defined but steady (the Quiescent Chiral State, QCS). Since this averaged pseudo-scalar does not vanish in a chiral fluid, any expansion of its distribution function must contain terms in this pseudo-scalar variable.

infographic.key_insight: A two-dimensional chiral fluid can generate an antisymmetric "chiral pressure" that comes from a parity-breaking pseudo-scalar and remains finite even in a homogeneous steady state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This identifies a zeroth-order constitutive effect that standard pressure models miss, which matters for CFD surrogates of micropolar, active, or chiral fluids.
method: Derived the microscopic expression for chiral pressure from the average pseudo-scalar in the fluid.
Connected the effect to rotational (vortex) viscosity in micropolar hydrodynamics.
Computed the kinetic rotational viscosity for rough disks to Gaussian order.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical derivation and kinetic calculation, showing that both chiral pressure and rotational viscosity persist at zeroth order in gradients and are compatible with a steady Quiescent Chiral State.
infographic.watch_item: The result is specialized to 2D chiral/rough-disk micropolar fluids, so direct use in conventional Navier-Stokes closures may require a tailored constitutive extension.
infographic.paper_title: Microscopic origin of the chiral pressure in a two-dimensional fluid

title: Rapid generation of relaxed centimeter-sized drops by capillary auto-ejection
authors: Patric Mueller, Kai Ihrig, Achim Sack, Jonathan E. Kollmer, Thorsten Poeschel
abstract: Many microgravity experiments require centimeter-sized spherical liquid drops. In drop-tower experiments, only a few seconds of microgravity are available, so the drops must be generated and reach a nearly relaxed state within a very short time. We investigate capillary auto-ejection (puddle jumping) as a passive mechanism for producing free-floating drops and investigate how the supporting cavity can be shaped to minimize the relaxation time after ejection. For cavities with a parabolic cross-section filled with a fixed liquid volume, minimization of the initial liquid surface area yields a unique shape, and smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations show that this shape also gives the shortest relaxation time within the parabolic family. Introducing a shallow central depression into the cavity reduces the relaxation time further, despite producing a larger initial liquid surface area. These results provide design principles for capillary-driven drop generators that enable the rapid production of relaxed centimeter-sized drops during the short microgravity intervals available in drop towers.

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing the cavity shape for capillary auto-ejection can generate centimeter-scale liquid drops that relax faster after ejection, making them suitable for short microgravity windows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical design rule for passive drop generators in drop-tower experiments, where drops must become nearly spherical within seconds.
method: Used a parabolic cavity filled with a fixed liquid volume and minimized the initial free-surface area.
Ran smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to compare relaxation times across cavity shapes.
Tested a modified shape with a shallow central depression to further accelerate relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation-based evaluation showing that the minimum-area parabolic shape gives the shortest relaxation time within that family, and that a shallow central depression improves it further.
infographic.watch_item: The best-performing depression shape may be sensitive to fabrication tolerances and liquid properties, so experimental validation is needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Rapid generation of relaxed centimeter-sized drops by capillary auto-ejection

title: Toward Principled Generative Data Assimilation of Turbulent Flows from Sparse Observations
authors: Baris Turan, Zhuoran Liu, Heng Xiao
abstract: Turbulent flows are highly chaotic, which makes their instantaneous states difficult to predict. Data assimilation aims to reduce this predictive uncertainty by synthesizing the predictions of a physical solver with partial observations of the system. Traditional data assimilation methods such as ensemble and variational approaches can incur substantial computational cost through evaluations of high-fidelity solvers and, for variational methods, adjoint calculations. Recently, generative diffusion models have been explored in the solution of inverse problems in fluid mechanics, demonstrating their potential for data assimilation. However, existing diffusion-based methods often use free parameters instead of the prescribed observation-error covariance to control the balance between the prior and likelihood, departing from the Bayesian formulation of data assimilation. We propose a framework for principled generative data assimilation in which observations are assimilated in the clean-state space and the prescribed observation-error covariance enters explicitly through an ensemble Kalman update. In the Lorenz-63 system, the proposed method yields a lower trajectory error and equation residual than the other diffusion-based posterior sampling methods considered, although its ensemble underestimates the posterior uncertainty. In two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the generated fields recover the statistics of the direct numerical simulation reference at large scales, with deviations confined to the smaller scales. These results suggest that the framework can produce physically plausible turbulent flow fields, indicating its potential for more challenging turbulent flow applications.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a principled diffusion-based data assimilation framework that incorporates observation-error covariance explicitly via an ensemble Kalman update in clean-state space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a more Bayesian, computationally practical route to reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse measurements without relying on ad hoc balance parameters.
method: Generate clean-state flow estimates with a diffusion model.
Assimilate sparse observations using an ensemble Kalman update with prescribed observation-error covariance.
Use the resulting posterior samples to reconstruct turbulent fields from partial data.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Lorenz-63, the method achieved lower trajectory error and equation residual than other diffusion-based posterior samplers, and in Rayleigh-Bénard convection it matched large-scale DNS statistics with small-scale deviations.
infographic.watch_item: The reported ensemble underestimates posterior uncertainty, so uncertainty quantification may be overconfident in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Principled Generative Data Assimilation of Turbulent Flows from Sparse Observations

title: On the transmission of floating-point perturbations in flow-dependent filter-width formulations in Large-Eddy Simulation
authors: Valerio D'Alessandro, Alessio Piccolo, Matteo Falone, Simone Bnà
abstract: Heterogeneous high--performance computing architectures expose numerical algorithms to perturbations arising from the non--associativity of floating--point arithmetic. In Large--Eddy Simulation (LES), similar numerical effects may become relevant when they affect the filter--width entering the subgrid scale (SGS) model. This work investigates this mechanism for the least--squares (LSQ) based filter--width formulation, focusing on how floating--point effects are generated, transmitted, and coupled with the resolved flow. We show that, for fixed resolved kinematics, the LSQ filter--width is logarithmically non-expansive but not strictly contractive with respect to perturbations of the mesh metrics. Consequently, small disturbances may be transmitted with little attenuation through strongly directional filter-width responses. To mitigate this sensitivity, we introduce a scalar max--min compression of the directional mesh scales together with a bounded modulation based on the resolved velocity gradient. The resulting formulation reroutes floating--point perturbations through the filter-width operator, improving robustness while preserving the flow--dependent character of the original LSQ construction. The framework is assessed on heterogeneous CPU and GPU architectures for flow past a circular cylinder at Re=3900 and the Taylor--Green vortex at Re=1600. In the former, nearly one--to--one transmission of relative metric disturbances can become relevant when the transmitted perturbations interact with shear-layer transition. By contrast, on orthogonal Taylor--Green vortex grids, the accumulation pathway is structurally absent and no comparable macroscopic response develops. These results suggest floating--point sensitivity matters for LES filter--width formulations in heterogeneous computing environments.

infographic.key_insight: Flow-dependent LES filter widths can pass floating-point perturbations through the SGS model with little attenuation, so numerical noise can become physically relevant on heterogeneous hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A robust max-min compressed, velocity-gradient-bounded filter-width formulation can reduce architecture-induced sensitivity while preserving flow dependence in LES.
method: Analyze how LSQ-based filter width transmits perturbations from mesh metrics
Introduce scalar max-min compression of directional mesh scales
Add bounded modulation from the resolved velocity gradient to reroute perturbations
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is evaluated on CPU and GPU for cylinder flow at Re=3900 and Taylor-Green vortex at Re=1600, showing strong transmission effects in the former and no comparable macroscopic response on orthogonal grids in the latter.
infographic.watch_item: The mitigation depends on mesh geometry and flow coupling, so gains may be limited or absent in configurations where the perturbation pathway is structurally weak.
infographic.paper_title: On the transmission of floating-point perturbations in flow-dependent filter-width formulations in Large-Eddy Simulation

title: Flow separation and turbulence production over trapezoidal protrusions
authors: Shahar Zuckerman, Jibu Tom Jose, Ori Levi, Omri Ram
abstract: The influence of rear-face inclination on turbulence around a surface-mounted protrusion depends on the separated flow approaching its trailing edge. This dependence is examined experimentally using stereoscopic particle image velocimetry over twelve trapezoidal protrusions with upper-surface length-to-height ratios $L/h=1,2,3,4$ and rear-face angles of $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, and $90^\circ$. Measurements were conducted at a height-based Reynolds number of approximately $5\times10^4$, with an incoming boundary-layer thickness comparable to the protrusion height. For $L/h=1$ and 2, a connected reverse-flow region extends over the upper surface into the wake. For $L/h=3$ and 4, upper-surface reattachment separates the two regions. Length governs this change in topology and the variation in turbulence levels at common spatial locations, whereas rear-face inclination has its strongest influence close to the surface. From $L/h=2$ onward, shallower faces have higher near-face turbulent kinetic energy, while vertical faces have lower energy but a larger spanwise fraction. A decomposition of the in-plane deviatoric production separates the effects of Reynolds-stress and mean-strain magnitudes from those of their relative principal-axis orientation. At the inclined faces, this contribution changes from negative to positive between $L/h=1$ and 2, before upper-surface reattachment occurs. Its subsequent increase with length is driven mainly by increasing tensor magnitudes, with the largest contribution at $L/h=4$ and $30^\circ$, where strong production remains close to the rear face. These results show that local turbulence production depends jointly on the flow state approaching the trailing edge and the position of the energetic shear layer relative to the rear surface.

infographic.key_insight: Rear-face turbulence production is controlled by how the separated flow reaches the trailing edge, with protrusion length causing a topology shift from connected reverse flow to upper-surface reattachment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Protrusion shape can be tuned to manage near-wall mixing and drag-related turbulence by changing the rear-face angle and upper-surface length.
method: Stereo PIV over 12 trapezoidal protrusions
Tested L/h = 1, 2, 3, 4 and rear-face angles of 30°, 45°, 90°
Analyzed Reynolds-stress, mean-strain, and deviatoric production contributions
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments at Re≈5×10^4 showed distinct changes in reverse-flow topology and turbulence levels, with length and rear-face inclination jointly governing production.
infographic.watch_item: The results are specific to a boundary layer thickness comparable to the protrusion height, so direct transfer to other Reynolds numbers or geometries should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Flow separation and turbulence production over trapezoidal protrusions

title: Helical pipes homogenize particle transport in pneumatic conveying
authors: Wing To Ku, Patric Mueller, Thorsten Poeschel
abstract: Pneumatic conveying at moderate gas velocities can result in strongly heterogeneous particle transport, with slow particles accumulating near the bottom of the pipe while faster particles are transported above. Here, we investigate helical pipes as a passive means of homogenizing particle transport without increasing the gas velocity. CFD-DEM simulations show that the helical pipe induces swirling motion of the gas and particles, continuously redistributing particles across the pipe cross-section. This transforms the heterogeneous transport observed in a straight pipe into a more homogeneous state with a narrower particle-velocity distribution. The results demonstrate that helical pipes can maintain efficient pneumatic conveying at moderate gas velocities while reducing excessive particle velocities.

infographic.key_insight: A helical pipe passively homogenizes pneumatic particle transport by inducing swirl that redistributes particles across the cross-section and narrows velocity differences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a geometry-based way to improve conveying uniformity at moderate gas velocities without increasing energy input or relying on active controls.
method: CFD-DEM simulations compare straight and helical pipe geometries.
The helical shape generates swirling gas and particle motion.
Cross-sectional mixing continuously redistributes particles during transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulation results in the abstract show the helical pipe transforms strongly heterogeneous transport into a more homogeneous state with a narrower particle-velocity distribution.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on pipe geometry and operating conditions, so pressure drop, wear, and scalability should be checked before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Helical pipes homogenize particle transport in pneumatic conveying

title: A conservative micro-continuum-cellular automaton method for multispecies biofilm dynamics in complex flows
authors: Soyoung Kim, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: We develop a conservative micro-continuum-cellular automaton method for simulating multispecies biofilm dynamics in complex flows. The proposed method couples the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes equations, reactive transport, suspended bacteria, and biofilm dynamics with a two-stage cellular automaton algorithm for biofilm redistribution and interface evolution. While treating biofilms as evolving porous media, we ensure conservative redistribution of multispecies biomass across partially occupied cells. Donor and recipient cell volumes are explicitly accounted for to conserve biomass and preserve species composition on non-uniform meshes. The proposed method is assessed against diffusion-dominated benchmark cases, including single-species fingering and multispecies stratification, and is further evaluated through a mesh-convergence study for flow and growth over a rectangular bump. The framework is then applied to counter-diffusional biofilms in a membrane-aerated biofilm reactor as a canonical example. The results demonstrate that the framework captures the expected biofilm morphology and stratification in systems involving coupled flow, substrate transport, and biofilm dynamics. The proposed method provides a flexible computational approach for simulating multispecies biofilm dynamics in complex flows and geometries.

infographic.key_insight: A conservative micro-continuum-cellular automaton framework can simulate multispecies biofilm growth, redistribution, and interface evolution in complex flows while preserving biomass and species composition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable prediction of biofilm behavior in reactors, porous media, and other flow systems where transport, growth, and morphology strongly interact.
method: Couples Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes flow with reactive transport, suspended bacteria, and biofilm dynamics.
Uses a two-stage cellular automaton to redistribute biomass and evolve the biofilm interface conservatively.
Accounts explicitly for donor/recipient cell volumes on non-uniform meshes to preserve multispecies composition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is evaluated on diffusion-dominated benchmarks, a mesh-convergence study over a rectangular bump, and a membrane-aerated biofilm reactor case, showing expected morphology and stratification.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and robustness may depend on careful treatment of partially occupied cells and mesh non-uniformity in the conservative redistribution step.
infographic.paper_title: A conservative micro-continuum-cellular automaton method for multispecies biofilm dynamics in complex flows

title: Scalar mixing by stagnation points on solid surfaces
authors: Gaute Linga, Tanguy Le Borgne, Joris Heyman
abstract: Recent advances have linked mixing in porous media to the deformation of infinitesimal fluid elements. However, these Lagrangian frameworks generally neglect or simplify interactions with solid surfaces. We consider transport of thin solute blobs (strips or sheets) near single generic obstacles, in particular along separation lines (separatrices) which connect to stagnation points at solid boundaries. In this case, we demonstrate that the coupling between flow and diffusion is analytically tractable. We provide a complete theory for scalar mixing near upstream stagnation points, which we validate by numerical simulations. We identify a mixing time scale $t_B \sim Pe^{1/3}$, where $Pe$ is the Péclet number, which controls whether scalar decay is driven by fluid stretching or by interaction with the solid boundary. Asymptotically, for times $t < t_B$, we find that the maximum concentration $c_{\rm max}$ decays as $t^{-5/2}$ and that the width $σ$ grows like $t^{1/2}$. For $t > t_B$, we find exponential decay of $c_{\rm max}$ and constant width $σ\sim s_B \sim Pe^{-1/3}$, where $s_B$ is a mixing length scale distinct from that which appears in shear flows. The asymptotic scalings of $c_{\rm max}(t)$ and $σ(t)$, and their dependence on $Pe$, are universal to no-slip stagnation points and qualitatively different from stagnation points in open flows.

infographic.key_insight: Near no-slip stagnation points on solid surfaces, solute mixing switches from stretch-dominated algebraic decay to boundary-controlled exponential decay at a universal Péclet-dependent crossover time $t_B\sim Pe^{1/3}$.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a predictive scaling law for contaminant transport and mixing near obstacles in porous media and wall-bounded flows, useful for designing reactors, filters, and remediation processes.
method: Analyze thin solute strips/sheets near separatrices ending at solid-boundary stagnation points
Derive asymptotic coupling between advection and diffusion near upstream stagnation points
Validate the theory against numerical simulations and extract scaling laws for $c_{\rm max}(t)$ and $\sigma(t)$
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a complete analytical theory that is explicitly validated by numerical simulations, with observed asymptotic scalings for concentration and width across regimes.
infographic.watch_item: The result is specialized to thin blobs near generic obstacles and no-slip stagnation points, so it may not transfer directly to open-flow stagnation points or more complex geometries without modification.
infographic.paper_title: Scalar mixing by stagnation points on solid surfaces

title: On the spectra of strong turbulence on water surfaces
authors: Gregory Falkovich
abstract: Here, I give a brief history of the theory, with twists and turns, and list possible predictions for the spectra of the direct cascade of gravity waves on the water. The description of long waves is straightforward within the weak-turbulence theory developed by Zakharov and his school. As the energy cascade proceeds to shorter scales, the mean surface steepness grows, and wave-breaking events appear with increasing frequency. Considering surface cusps, Phillips suggested a wavenumber spectrum (with a wrong magnitude, as I argue here) and a frequency spectrum whose whole form is incorrect. The right form for the frequency spectral slope due to breaking waves was suggested by Kuznetsov. Here we estimate the magnitude and argue that the frequency spectrum is expected to continue unchanged through the whole cascade. The transition from weak to strong turbulence in the wavenumber and spatio-temporal spectra is due to spectrally nonlocal interactions and happens earlier (at larger scales) than the dimensional estimate suggests. As a result, the magnitude of the strong-turbulence spectrum is not universal but depends on the pumping for a sufficiently long weak-turbulence cascade. The reason for nonlocality is likely that breaking of shorter waves is determined by the magnitude of the longest wave on whose crest they are running.

infographic.key_insight: Strong-water-wave turbulence transitions from weak-turbulence scaling to breaking-wave-dominated spectra earlier than expected, and the resulting strong-turbulence spectrum is non-universal because it depends on pumping and nonlocal interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps predict ocean surface energy spectra and wave-breaking behavior, which matter for remote sensing, coastal engineering, and air-sea interaction models.
method: Review weak-turbulence theory for long gravity waves.
Estimate spectra in the breaking-wave regime using cusp-based arguments and Kuznetsov’s frequency-slope prediction.
Assess how nonlocal interactions shift the weak-to-strong turbulence transition across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a theoretical synthesis and scaling analysis based on prior theory and spectral arguments rather than new experimental data.
infographic.watch_item: The strong-turbulence spectrum may not be universal, so predictions can vary with forcing/pumping conditions and should not be applied without context.
infographic.paper_title: On the spectra of strong turbulence on water surfaces

title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
authors: Seongkyu Lee
abstract: Porous and perforated leading edges reduce turbulence-interaction noise, but predictions of the reduction have relied on material impedances adjusted to the acoustic data. This paper removes that adjustment. The finite-chord scattering problem is solved in compressible subsonic flow for an arbitrary chordwise admittance, with the shed wake, the Kutta condition and permeability-dependent edge singularities, and closed to the far field with the finite span and the array aperture represented. The admittance of a perforated insert is derived from the Rayleigh conductivity of one aperture with three computed corrections: plate thickness, interaction between neighbouring apertures, and Howe's grazing-flow blockage evaluated at the aperture-averaged velocity of the boundary layer. A bulk porous insert is represented by its measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia. For three perforates at four flow conditions the prediction agrees with measurements to 2.5 dB rms over 84 comparisons, against 4.4 dB with the unscaled impedance used previously. Although the Mach number is 0.05, the chord is acoustically non-compact, and an incompressible solution rises where the measurement falls. Two of three bulk porous inserts are predicted to within 1.7 dB rms where interaction noise dominates. Narrow, equally spaced peaks measured on perforated plates are reproduced by none of the admittances tested; their spacing implies a source convecting at 0.62 of the free-stream speed, absent from a frozen-gust model. A parameter study shows that the perforate geometry acts almost entirely through one low-frequency admittance group, in which the hole radius cancels for holes buried in the laminar boundary layer.

infographic.key_insight: A finite-chord compressible scattering model predicts leading-edge noise reduction for perforated and porous inserts without fitted acoustic constants by deriving the insert admittance from measurable geometry and flow physics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable design of low-noise airfoil leading edges for turbomachinery and aeroacoustics, with better transfer from test data to real hardware.
method: Solved the finite-chord, compressible subsonic leading-edge scattering problem with arbitrary chordwise admittance, including wake shedding, Kutta condition, and permeability-dependent edge singularities.
Derived perforated-insert admittance from Rayleigh conductivity with corrections for plate thickness, aperture interaction, and grazing-flow blockage.
Modeled bulk porous inserts using measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia, then closed the far field with finite-span and array-aperture effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: For three perforated inserts across four flow conditions, the model matched measurements to 2.5 dB rms over 84 comparisons versus 4.4 dB for the earlier scaled-impedance approach; two of three porous inserts were predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
infographic.watch_item: A narrow tonal peak pattern seen on perforated plates was not captured by the tested admittances, suggesting an additional convecting source mechanism beyond the frozen-gust assumption.
infographic.paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants

title: Direct Modeling of Pore Size Evolution and Microcollapse in Lyophilization by Population Balance
authors: Isaac Stonewall Wheeler, Vivek Narsimhan, Alina A. Alexeenko, Davide Fissore
abstract: In the primary drying step of pharmaceutical freeze drying, it is well known that amorphous excipients are prone to "microcollapse" as they approach their glass transition temperature. Existing modeling approaches for this phenomenon generally entail either avoidance of this regime or an experimentally burdensome empirical assessment of the resulting drop in resistance to mass transfer. In this work, we approach the phenomenon head-on by developing a population balance model for the pore size distribution of a freeze-dried cake during microcollapse and relating the pore size to mass transfer resistance. By treating the population balance with the method of moments and an interpolative closure, we keep the model's computational burden on par with the literature-standard model for primary drying. For a literature example when mass transfer resistance clearly varies as a function of product temperature during drying, we fit the population balance model to cases with high and low product temperature and show that it can then simulate intermediate cases with equal accuracy. The validity of the expression for mass transfer resistance is demonstrated with another literature data set, where pore size distributions were measured after the fact for a formulation without microcollapse; only a single parameter from this model needs to be fit to those cases to yield predictive accuracy in product temperature on par with post-hoc empirical assessment. Finally, a sophisticated multi-experiment fit for one formulation across a range of conditions yields quantitative agreement in product temperatures, suggesting that the rate constant for microcollapse behavior may be a material parameter and independent of the precise porous geometry.

infographic.key_insight: A population balance model can directly track pore size evolution during lyophilization microcollapse and translate it into mass-transfer resistance with predictive accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a computationally light way to forecast product temperature and drying behavior in freeze-drying, reducing reliance on empirical post-hoc resistance fitting.
method: Model pore-size distribution with a population balance equation during primary drying.
Apply the method of moments with interpolative closure to keep computation comparable to standard drying models.
Link pore size evolution to mass-transfer resistance and fit only limited parameters to experimental data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model matched literature cases with both high and low product temperatures, predicted intermediate cases, and agreed quantitatively with multi-experiment data across a range of conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on calibration of microcollapse kinetics and resistance parameters, so transferability across formulations may require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Modeling of Pore Size Evolution and Microcollapse in Lyophilization by Population Balance

title: Flow-rate controls on trapped hydrogen redistribution in a heterogeneous sandstone: a synchrotron X-ray micro-CT study
authors: Catherine Spurin, Sojwal Manoorkar, Sharon Ellman, Ian B. Butler, Aliakbar Hassanpouryouzband, Damien Freitas
abstract: Subsurface hydrogen storage in porous geological formations is a promising strategy for balancing temporal mismatches between renewable energy generation and demand. The viability of large-scale hydrogen storage depends on predicting hydrogen distribution, trapping, and recovery during cyclic injection and withdrawal operations. However, these multiphase flow processes are influenced by rock heterogeneity, capillary hysteresis and trapping at the pore-scale. In this work, fast in-situ synchrotron X-ray tomography was used to directly visualise hydrogen mobilisation during brine imbibition in a heterogeneous sandstone. By systematically varying the brine injection rate, the influence of flow conditions on hydrogen recovery, and the evolution of trapped hydrogen were quantified. Significant mobilisation of disconnected hydrogen clusters was observed during imbibition, even at low capillary numbers ($< 10^{-6}$). Rock heterogeneity influenced trapping behaviour, particularly during the early stages of imbibition. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating pore-scale heterogeneity and transient trapping mechanisms into hydrogen storage predictions.

infographic.key_insight: Brine injection rate strongly affects how much trapped hydrogen is remobilized in heterogeneous sandstone, even under very low capillary-number flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hydrogen storage models must include pore-scale heterogeneity and transient trapping/recovery effects to predict cyclic inject-withdraw performance reliably.
method: Fast in-situ synchrotron X-ray micro-CT tracked hydrogen redistribution during brine imbibition.
Brine injection rate was systematically varied to test flow-rate dependence.
Trapped hydrogen cluster evolution and recovery were quantified in a heterogeneous sandstone sample.
infographic.evidence_signal: Micro-CT observations showed significant mobilization of disconnected hydrogen clusters during imbibition, including at capillary numbers below 10^-6.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from pore-scale imaging of a heterogeneous sandstone, so field-scale predictions still need upscaling and rock-specific validation.
infographic.paper_title: Flow-rate controls on trapped hydrogen redistribution in a heterogeneous sandstone: a synchrotron X-ray micro-CT study

title: A Reynolds-like Criterion for the Onset of Universal Active Turbulence
authors: Kunal Kumar, Sandip Sahoo, Kirti Kashyap, Amal Manoharan, Siddhartha Mukherjee, Anupam Gupta
abstract: Beyond a critical Toner--Tu drive, bacterial turbulence exhibits universal statistics, including a parameter-independent energy spectrum $E(k)\sim k^{-3/2}$. We show that the same universal state can be reached not only by increasing activity, but also by strengthening nonlinear advection, weakening nonlinear saturation, or tuning the Swift--Hohenberg instability. Motivated by the competition between these processes, we identify the independent dimensionless groups governing the dynamics and construct a Reynolds-like control parameter from them. A single critical value, calibrated from the known activity-controlled transition, predicts the onset of universality along the other parameter routes and collapses them onto a common threshold. These results identify a dynamical organizing parameter for the onset of universal active turbulence and provide a Reynolds-like measure for the Toner--Tu--Swift--Hohenberg universality class.

infographic.key_insight: The paper identifies a Reynolds-like dimensionless control parameter that predicts when active turbulence enters a universal regime, regardless of whether the transition is driven by stronger activity, advection, weaker saturation, or instability tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a single practical threshold for comparing and designing active-fluid systems across different parameter routes, helping engineers predict onset conditions for universal turbulent behavior.
method: Isolate the independent dimensionless groups in the Toner--Tu--Swift--Hohenberg dynamics.
Construct a composite Reynolds-like parameter from the balance of drive, nonlinear advection, saturation, and instability effects.
Calibrate one critical threshold using the known activity-driven transition and test it on other control routes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the proposed parameter collapses multiple transition pathways onto a common critical value and matches the known universal state with the parameter-independent spectrum E(k) ~ k^-3/2.
infographic.watch_item: The threshold is calibrated from one known transition, so its robustness may depend on how broadly the same universality class assumptions hold in experiments or simulations.
infographic.paper_title: A Reynolds-like Criterion for the Onset of Universal Active Turbulence

title: Generalised Mixing-Plane Method for Compressible Reacting-Mixture Flows in Steady Multiphysics Turbomachinery Simulations
authors: Yifeng Wang, Lin Shi, Fenglai Huang, Rui Wang, Feng Wang, Hui Xu
abstract: The mixing-plane method plays a pivotal role in steady simulations of multiple turbomachinery components. With advances in computational power, a whole-engine gas turbine simulation is no longer an elusive approach. However, whole-engine simulations require simultaneous coupling of the compressor, turbine and combustor. A key challenge is that the working fluid after the combustor can no longer be treated as a perfect gas, since the combustion introduces composition variations and combustion products. Conventional mixing-plane methods based on a fixed-composition gas cannot guarantee a thermodynamically consistent mixed-out state. To overcome the difficulty, this paper extends the classic mixing-plane approach to handle compressible reacting flows. The nonlinearity in the thermodynamic closure is addressed using a novel nested algorithm combining an outer pressure-root search with an inner enthalpy inversion. Physical state checks and power-law pressure sampling are incorporated to improve numerical robustness at low normal velocities where the pressure root approaches its upper physical bound. The performance of the method is demonstrated in three configurations: a quasi-1D interface test elucidating the thermodynamic stiffness of the proposed mixing-plane formulation for different fuel types and flow conditions; the Darmstadt transonic compressor case that verifies the proposed method reduces to the classic mixing-plane formulation when the mixture fraction reduces to zero; and a whole-engine simulation of the KJ66 micro-turbojet is used to demonstrate the performance of the method for multiphysics turbomachinery simulations. Good agreement with experimental data is observed, and the maximum relative mass-flow error across the mixing planes remains below 0.11%, demonstrating conservative and thermodynamically consistent interface coupling for compressible reacting turbomachinery flows.

infographic.key_insight: The paper extends the classic mixing-plane interface to compressible reacting-mixture flows by enforcing a thermodynamically consistent mixed-out state through nested pressure and enthalpy solves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables steady whole-engine turbomachinery simulations that couple compressor, combustor, and turbine without losing conservation or physical consistency across composition-changing interfaces.
method: Outer search for the interface pressure root.
Inner enthalpy inversion to recover the mixed thermodynamic state.
Physical-state checks plus power-law pressure sampling for robustness near low normal velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated on a quasi-1D interface test, a Darmstadt transonic compressor case, and a KJ66 micro-turbojet whole-engine simulation, with maximum relative mass-flow error below 0.11% across mixing planes.
infographic.watch_item: The nested nonlinear solve can become stiff near low normal velocities, so robust root-bracketing and state validation are important in implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Generalised Mixing-Plane Method for Compressible Reacting-Mixture Flows in Steady Multiphysics Turbomachinery Simulations
